paragraphs: When the people of America reflect that they are now called upon to decide a question whose consequences must prove among the most important that ever engaged their attention, it will be evident that they should take a view of it that is both very comprehensive and very serious.

Nothing is more certain than the indispensable necessity of government, and it is equally undeniable that, whenever and however it is instituted, the people must give up some of their natural rights in order to give it the powers it requires. It is therefore well worth considering whether it would serve the interest of the people of America better to be, for all general purposes, one nation under one federal government, or to divide themselves into separate confederacies and give to the head of each the same kind of powers that they are advised to place in one national government.

Until recently it was a received and uncontradicted opinion that the prosperity of the people of America depended on their remaining firmly united, and the wishes, prayers, and efforts of our best and wisest citizens have constantly been directed to that goal. But politicians now appear who insist that this opinion is mistaken, and that instead of looking for safety and happiness in union, we ought to seek them in a division of the States into distinct confederacies or sovereignties. However extraordinary this new doctrine may seem, it has its advocates, and certain persons who formerly opposed it strongly are now among them. Whatever arguments or inducements have brought about this change in the views and declarations of these gentlemen, it certainly would not be wise for the people at large to adopt these new political tenets without being fully convinced that they rest on truth and sound policy.

It has often given me pleasure to observe that independent America was not made up of detached and distant territories, but that one connected, fertile, wide-spreading country was the portion of our western sons of liberty. Providence has blessed it in a special way with a variety of soils and products, and has watered it with countless streams for the delight and convenience of its inhabitants. A succession of navigable waters forms a kind of chain around its borders, as if to bind it together, while the noblest rivers in the world, running at convenient distances, offer the people highways for the easy exchange of friendly aid and for the mutual transport and trade of their various goods.

With equal pleasure I have as often noticed that Providence has been pleased to give this one connected country to one united people. They are a people descended from the same ancestors, speaking the same language, professing the same religion, attached to the same principles of government, and very similar in their manners and customs. By their joint counsels, arms, and efforts, fighting side by side through a long and bloody war, they have nobly established general liberty and independence.

This country and this people seem to have been made for each other, and it appears to have been the design of Providence that an inheritance so suitable and convenient for a band of brothers, joined to one another by the strongest ties, should never be split into a number of unsociable, jealous, and alien sovereignties.

Similar views have until now prevailed among all ranks and denominations of men among us. For all general purposes we have uniformly been one people, each individual citizen everywhere enjoying the same national rights, privileges, and protection. As a nation we have made peace and war; as a nation we have defeated our common enemies; as a nation we have formed alliances, made treaties, and entered into various compacts and conventions with foreign states.

A strong sense of the value and blessings of union led the people, at a very early period, to establish a federal government to preserve and perpetuate it. They formed it almost as soon as they had a political existence. Indeed, they formed it at a time when their homes were in flames, when many of their citizens were bleeding, and when the progress of hostility and devastation left little room for the calm and mature inquiries and reflections that must always precede the formation of a wise and well-balanced government for a free people. It is not to be wondered at that a government established in such unfavorable times should, when tried, be found greatly deficient and inadequate to the purpose it was meant to serve.

This intelligent people saw and regretted these defects. They remained as attached to union as they were devoted to liberty, and they saw that the former was in immediate danger and the latter in more remote danger. Being persuaded that ample security for both could be found only in a more wisely framed national government, they convened, as with one voice, the recent convention at Philadelphia to take that important subject under consideration.

This convention was composed of men who possessed the confidence of the people, many of whom had become highly distinguished for their patriotism, virtue and wisdom in times that tried the minds and hearts of men. They undertook the difficult task. In the gentle season of peace, with minds unoccupied by other subjects, they spent many months in calm, uninterrupted, daily consultation. Finally, without having been overawed by power or influenced by any passion except love for their country, they presented and recommended to the people the plan produced by their joint and very unanimous counsels.

Grant that this plan is only RECOMMENDED, not imposed, which is the fact. Yet let it be remembered that it is recommended neither to BLIND approval nor to BLIND rejection, but to that calm and fair consideration which the magnitude and importance of the subject demand and which it certainly ought to receive. But (as was remarked in the preceding number of this series) it is more to be wished than expected that it will be so considered and examined. Experience on a former occasion teaches us not to be too hopeful about this. It is not yet forgotten that well-founded fears of imminent danger led the people of America to form the memorable Congress of 1774. That body recommended certain measures to their constituents, and events proved its wisdom. Yet it is fresh in our memories how soon the press began to swarm with pamphlets and weekly papers against those very measures. Not only many officers of government, who obeyed the dictates of personal interest, but others as well, from a mistaken estimate of consequences, or the undue influence of former attachments, or an ambition aimed at objects that did not correspond with the public good, were tireless in their efforts to persuade the people to reject the advice of that patriotic Congress. Many, indeed, were deceived and misled, but the great majority of the people reasoned and decided wisely, and they are happy in reflecting that they did so.

They considered that the Congress was composed of many wise and experienced men. They considered that, having been brought together from different parts of the country, those men brought with them, and shared with one another, a variety of useful information. They considered that, in the time they spent together inquiring into and discussing the true interests of their country, they must have acquired very accurate knowledge on that subject. And they considered that those men were each personally concerned in the public liberty and prosperity, and that it was therefore no less their inclination than their duty to recommend only such measures as, after the most mature deliberation, they really thought prudent and advisable.

These and similar considerations then led the people to rely greatly on the judgment and integrity of the Congress, and they took its advice despite the various arts and efforts used to deter them from it. But if the people at large had reason to trust the men of that Congress, few of whom had been fully tested or generally known, they now have still greater reason to respect the judgment and advice of the convention. For it is well known that some of the most distinguished members of that Congress, who have since been tested and rightly approved for patriotism and ability, and who have grown old in acquiring political knowledge, were also members of this convention and carried into it their accumulated knowledge and experience.

It is worth remarking that not only the first Congress but every Congress since, as well as the recent convention, have invariably joined with the people in thinking that the prosperity of America depended on its Union. To preserve and perpetuate it was the great object of the people in forming that convention, and it is also the great object of the plan that the convention has advised them to adopt. With what propriety, then, or for what good purposes, do some men at this particular time attempt to belittle the importance of the Union? Or why is it suggested that three or four confederacies would be better than one? I am persuaded in my own mind that the people have always thought rightly on this subject, and that their universal and uniform attachment to the cause of the Union rests on great and weighty reasons, which I shall endeavor to develop and explain in some of the following papers. Those who promote the idea of putting a number of distinct confederacies in place of the plan of the convention seem clearly to foresee that rejecting it would put the continuance of the Union in the utmost jeopardy. That certainly would be the case, and I sincerely wish that every good citizen may foresee as clearly that, whenever the dissolution of the Union arrives, America will have reason to exclaim, in the words of the poet: "FAREWELL! A LONG FAREWELL TO ALL MY GREATNESS."
